summary: Psalm 109 begins with a speaker asking God not to stay silent while enemies attack him with lies, hatred, and evil returned for love. The center of the psalm gives a long, severe appeal for judgment against an adversary and his household, then explains that the adversary persecuted the poor and needy and loved cursing. The final movement returns to the speaker’s own weakness and asks Yahweh to save him, ending with public thanks because Yahweh stands beside the needy against those who judge them.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows the Psalter making room for rage, accusation, bodily distress, and trust in God’s judgment. It is one of the starkest examples of imprecatory prayer, so readers need to face both its pain and its moral difficulty without turning it into a simple model for private revenge.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by David,” but Psalms headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, collection, or reception, and their precise historical force is debated.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also using the Psalms for prayer and interpretation.
context.date: The Psalms are a many-period anthology; individual poems may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period, and one date for the whole book would be misleading.
context.setting: Psalm 109 is in Book V of the Psalter. The poem itself speaks from a crisis of slander, accusation, poverty, weakness, and public reproach, without naming one historical event.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic prayer of complaint, curse, petition, and praise, shaped by parallel lines, repeated appeals, and vivid images.

outline.heading: Do not be silent
outline.note: The speaker calls on the God of his praise while enemies answer his love with deceit, hatred, and evil.

outline.heading: Judgment requested
outline.note: A severe series of petitions asks that an adversary be condemned, lose office, lose household security, and have his memory cut off.

outline.heading: Why judgment is sought
outline.note: The psalm says the adversary refused kindness, persecuted the poor and brokenhearted, loved cursing, and spoke evil against the speaker’s soul.

outline.heading: The wounded speaker asks for help
outline.note: The speaker appeals to Yahweh’s name and loving kindness, describing poverty, bodily weakness, fasting, and public shame.

outline.heading: Curse answered by blessing
outline.note: The psalm contrasts enemy cursing with God’s blessing and closes with the speaker’s promise of public thanks because Yahweh stands at the right hand of the needy.

keyVerses.text: In return for my love, they are my adversaries; but I am in prayer.
keyVerses.why: This line states the central wound of the opening: love has been answered by opposition, and the speaker’s response is directed toward prayer.

keyVerses.text: Let his days be few. Let another take his office.
keyVerses.why: This verse is a compact example of the psalm’s judgment petitions. It also became important in later Christian reception, where Acts applies it to Judas, though Psalm 109 itself does not name him.

keyVerses.text: But deal with me, Yahweh the Lord, for your name’s sake, because your loving kindness is good, deliver me;
keyVerses.why: After the curses, the speaker turns directly to Yahweh for deliverance grounded in God’s name and loving kindness.

keyVerses.text: For he will stand at the right hand of the needy, to save him from those who judge his soul.
keyVerses.why: The closing line gives the psalm’s final confidence: God is pictured beside the needy person against hostile judgment.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading says the psalm is “by David,” but headings in Psalms can signal several kinds of relationship, including authorship, association, dedication, or belonging. Inside the poem, the speaker is an afflicted worshiper who is opposed by enemies, prays to God, and calls himself poor, needy, and God’s servant.

questions.question: What has been done to the speaker?
questions.answer: The speaker says enemies have attacked him with wicked, deceitful, lying, and hateful words. He also says they fought him without cause and repaid his love and good with hatred and evil. The psalm presents the crisis mainly as verbal, social, and legal hostility, not as a narrated battle scene.

questions.question: Why are verses 6-20 so harsh?
questions.answer: These verses ask God to bring ruin on an adversary, his work, his family, and his memory. The psalm gives a reason in verses 16-18: the adversary did not show kindness, persecuted the poor and needy, and loved cursing. Readers differ over how to use such prayers: some emphasize that the speaker hands judgment to God rather than acting it out, while others stress the moral shock of the requested harm, especially toward children.

questions.question: What does “adversary” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter an adversary is someone standing against the speaker. The word appears in the opening complaint, in the request that an adversary stand at the accused person’s right hand, and again when the speaker names those who oppose him. The chapter uses courtroom-like and conflict language, but it does not identify the adversary by name.

questions.question: Does the psalm say the speaker is innocent?
questions.answer: The speaker says the attacks are “without a cause” and that he has offered love and good while receiving hatred and evil. The psalm does not provide a full case file or an outside narrator’s investigation. It gives the prayer of a sufferer who brings his own account before God.

questions.question: What is meant by “Let another take his office”?
questions.answer: In the psalm, the line belongs to a curse asking that the adversary’s life be shortened and his position pass to someone else. Later Christian readers connect this verse with Judas through Acts, and that reception matters historically. Psalm 109 itself, however, does not name Judas or describe the events of the New Testament.

questions.question: Why does the psalm talk about children, wife, parents, and posterity?
questions.answer: The curse section imagines judgment reaching beyond the adversary himself into household, inheritance, and public memory. That is one reason the psalm is difficult for many readers. The chapter’s own explanation focuses on the adversary’s refusal of kindness and persecution of the vulnerable, but it does not remove the disturbing force of the words about family.

questions.question: How does the speaker describe his own suffering?
questions.answer: He says he is poor and needy, wounded in heart, fading like an evening shadow, shaken off like a locust, weakened by fasting, and visibly thin. He also says he has become a reproach to his enemies, who shake their heads when they see him. The psalm links inner distress, bodily weakness, and public shame.

questions.question: How does the psalm end after so much cursing?
questions.answer: It ends with a contrast: enemies may curse, but God blesses. The speaker expects shame for the adversaries, joy for God’s servant, and public praise among the multitude. The final reason is that Yahweh stands at the right hand of the needy to save him from those who judge his soul.

glossary.def: The opening heading addresses the psalm for performance or use connected with music, though the exact ancient setting is not explained in the chapter.
In this psalm the word describes those whose speech and actions oppose the speaker; it appears in the complaint and in the judgment request.
People who stand against the speaker. The psalm uses the term for those who return his love with opposition and speak evil against his soul.
The speaker appeals to Yahweh’s loving kindness as the ground for deliverance, especially in verses 21 and 26.
A phrase used for the vulnerable person persecuted by the adversary and for the speaker’s own condition before God.
